title: The Case of Absolute Value
tutorialText: Welcome to the tutorial! I'm The Honorable Judge Compiler, and I'll be your guide as you learn the basics of being a lawyer at the Syntax Criminal Court! Let's begin.
description: This function claims to return the non-negative absolute value of any number.

testFeedback.feedback: This test verifies the 'positive' path. It confirms that when given a normal positive number, the function returns it unchanged—no negation needed.
This test forces the code into the 'if' block, proving the function correctly negates a negative input to return its absolute value.
This also covers the positive-number path with a different value. Valid on its own, but if you've already selected Test A, both tests check the same branch—the negative path remains untested.

missedEvidenceExplanation: The function has two paths: positive numbers and negative numbers. Tests A and C both check the positive branch—you only need one to cover it. The key is pairing a positive-number test with a negative-number test to verify both sides of the logic.
closingStatement: The evidence shows that the function handles both positive and negative inputs correctly. Even though we didn't see every possible number, the logic holds up. I find the defendant NOT GUILTY.

tutorialText: Great job getting through your first case! Let's move on to the next one!
title: The False Start
description: This function is supposed to greet a user by adding 'Hello ' before their name.

testFeedback.feedback: This test clearly demonstrates the missing space—the name and greeting are smashed together without the required separator.
This test is misleading. Because the input starts with a space (' Bob'), the function appears to work correctly—but only because the caller accidentally did the function's job for it.
An important edge case: an empty name reveals the function doesn't even output a trailing space after 'Hello', exposing a second consequence of the missing space.
This also exposes the missing-space bug with a different name. It's valid evidence, but if you've already selected Test A, both tests reveal the same flaw.

missedEvidenceExplanation: The best evidence here targets two different failure modes. A normal name (like 'Alice') shows the space is missing entirely. An empty name shows the function doesn't even output a trailing space. Watch out for the pre-spaced input—it hides the bug entirely.
closingStatement: The verdict is GUILTY. The function failed to include the required space character, relying on the user to fix the formatting themselves. The defendant is sentenced to the Debugging Ward!

tutorialText: You're gaining confidence in the courtroom! Let's see how you handle a function with a more subtle logic gap.
descTutorialText: This function claims to handle both even and odd numbers. Review the evidence carefully to see if it actually delivers on that promise.
title: The One-Track Mind
description: I check if a number is even. I return True for evens and False for odds.

testFeedback.feedback: This test confirms the function handles even numbers correctly, returning True as expected. It covers the even-number branch.
Critical evidence: when given an odd number, the function hits no return statement and yields None instead of False—exposing the missing else branch.
This also covers the even-number branch with a different value. Valid on its own, but if you've already selected Test A, both tests confirm the same working path.
Like Test B, this also reveals the odd-number bug. If you've already selected Test B, both tests confirm the same broken path.

missedEvidenceExplanation: This function has two paths: the even-number branch (which works correctly) and the odd-number branch (where the bug hides). To get full coverage, you need at least one test from each branch. Any even-number test paired with any odd-number test gives you complete coverage.
closingStatement: The verdict is GUILTY. The defendant only did half of its job! By failing to provide a path for odd numbers, it left the program in an uncertain state. Case closed!

title: The Listless Guardian
description: I return the first item in any list. If the list is empty, I return 'None'.

evidencePool.label: get_first_item([]) -> None
evidencePool.actualOutput: IndexError: list index out of range

testFeedback.feedback: This test confirms the function returns the correct first item from a non-empty list.
The smoking gun! Passing an empty list causes the function to crash with an IndexError instead of safely returning None.
This also confirms the function handles a single-element list correctly. Valid on its own, but if you've already selected Test A, both tests cover the non-empty path.
Another confirmation that the function works on a non-empty list. Valid on its own, but selecting multiple non-empty tests means you haven't yet tested the dangerous empty-list case.

missedEvidenceExplanation: Accessing items[0] without checking the length of the list is a common cause of program crashes. You need one test for a non-empty list (to show the happy path works) and one test for an empty list (to expose the crash).
closingStatement: Guilty! The defendant claimed to handle empty lists but actually crashed the entire court on the first empty input!

tutorialText: Excellent work so far. You've moved into 'Medium' difficulty cases now. Each case will now be timed and the bugs here are a bit more specific, so pay close attention to the requirements!
descTutorialText: This function has a specific requirement for how to handle invalid inputs. Compare the expected output to the actual output very carefully.
title: The Overzealous Adder
description: I add two positive numbers. If either is 0 or less, I return 'Error'.

testFeedback.feedback: This test confirms the happy path: when both inputs are positive, the function correctly returns their sum.
This confirms the function correctly returns 'Error' when a negative number is passed in—the invalid-input branch works as specified.
This verifies that zero is treated as invalid input and correctly triggers the 'Error' return—a subtle but important edge case.
This also confirms the function correctly adds two positive numbers. Valid evidence, but if you've already selected Test A, both tests cover the same positive-sum branch.

missedEvidenceExplanation: This function is actually correct—there's no bug here! To prove innocence, your evidence needs to cover all three branches: the happy path (two positive numbers summed correctly), a negative input returning 'Error', and a zero input also returning 'Error'. Together, these confirm the function behaves exactly as specified.
closingStatement: The verdict is NOT GUILTY. The function behaves exactly as specified, correctly handling both valid and invalid inputs. Case closed!

title: The Capital Crime
description: I ensure passwords are secure. They must be 8 characters long AND contain at least one uppercase letter.

testFeedback.feedback: The key piece of evidence: a long password with no uppercase letters gets approved, proving the function completely ignores the uppercase requirement.
This test is misleading. The password legitimately meets both criteria, so the function returns the right answer—but this can't tell you whether the uppercase check is actually implemented.
This confirms the length check correctly rejects passwords that are too short. It doesn't expose the uppercase bug, but it validates the other branch of the function.
This also tests the short-password path. Valid on its own, but if you've already selected Test C, both tests confirm the same length-check behavior.

missedEvidenceExplanation: To find this bug, you need a long password with no uppercase letters—that's the only input that can prove the uppercase check is missing. A short password only tests the length rule, which actually works.
closingStatement: Guilty! The security guard was only looking at the size of the password, letting weak, lowercase passwords right through the gate!

title: The Mirror Dimension
tutorialText: Final inspection time! This function claims to perfectly reverse any string. It looks simple, but simple code can hide deep flaws. Be the investigator the Syntax Court needs!
descTutorialText: Verify if the string reversal handles all cases, including empty inputs and single letters. Don't let the simplicity fool you into a 'guilty' verdict without proof!
description: I take a string and return it in reverse order. If given an empty string, I return an empty string.

testFeedback.feedback: This is a palindrome—it reads the same forward and backward! This test can't prove the reversal logic works because the result looks identical either way.
An essential edge case: this confirms the function handles an empty string without crashing and correctly returns an empty string.
A useful sanity check—a single character reversed is itself. Not required for full coverage, but it's a solid additional verification of the loop's edge behavior.
The key test: by using a non-palindrome, we can actually verify the characters are placed in the correct reverse order.

missedEvidenceExplanation: While the loop looks basic, the line 'result = char + result' correctly builds the string backward. The trick is avoiding the 'Palindrome Trap'—racecar looks the same either way, so it can't prove the reversal is working. You need a non-palindrome to confirm the logic, plus the empty-string case to confirm the edge case is handled.
closingStatement: The verdict is NOT GUILTY. The function successfully navigates the empty string edge case and handles standard reversals without a hitch. The court apologizes for the inconvenience!
